lessons.title: Common Pitfalls: Non-Convexity, Infeasibility, and Numerical Instability

children.text: A solver does not fail randomly. Every common failure traces back to one specific assumption this course spent six chapters establishing, now broken. Recognizing which one broke is the difference between staring at a cryptic error message and knowing exactly what to fix.

body.text: Every common solver failure traces back to a specific broken assumption this course established. Recognizing which one broke tells you exactly how to fix it, instead of guessing.

children.text: Chapter 2 named the usual culprits directly: cardinality limits (hold at most K stocks), minimum-holding thresholds (either 0 or at least X%), and any other all-or-nothing or discrete counting rule. The telltale symptom is running the same optimization from different starting points and getting different answers, each reported as merely local, or a solver that runs far longer than a QP of this size should, hunting through a landscape with more than one valley. The fix is rarely to force the plain machinery of this course to work anyway. It is to reformulate: relax the discrete rule into a continuous approximation and solve that convex version, or hand the problem to a dedicated mixed-integer solver built for exactly this kind of constraint.

Chapter 1 defined the feasible region as every point satisfying all constraints at once. Infeasibility means that region is empty, literally no portfolio satisfies every rule simultaneously. A target return set higher than any achievable combination can reach, even with full leverage, is one common cause. Contradictory constraints are another, and easier to miss: a mandate requiring at least 40% in banking stocks alongside a separate rule capping banking exposure at 30% is not solvable by any portfolio, no matter how sophisticated the solver. Most solvers report infeasibility directly rather than failing silently, but finding which specific constraints conflict usually means relaxing them one at a time and re-solving until the conflict disappears.

Chapter 2 proved every genuine covariance matrix is positive semi-definite. Estimated covariance matrices, built from real historical data, are a different story. Estimating an N-asset covariance matrix needs roughly N(N+1)/2 independent numbers, and with only T historical time periods of data, T needs to comfortably exceed N for that estimate to be stable. When T is close to N, or worse, smaller than N, the estimated matrix becomes ill-conditioned, or even technically singular, mathematically still PSD in theory but so close to the boundary that tiny estimation noise gets massively amplified once it is inverted.

The symptom is distinctive: weights that swing to extreme, often implausible values, large long and short positions that do not survive re-running the estimate with one extra week of data. This is the same fragility flagged in Chapter 2's discussion of shrinkage estimators. The standard fixes shrink the noisy sample covariance matrix toward a simpler, more stable target, or replace it with a factor model that estimates far fewer independent parameters from the same data.

cells: Different answers from different starting points; "local" status
A cardinality, minimum-holding, or other discrete rule (Chapter 2)
Constraints that cannot all be satisfied at once (Chapter 1)
Extreme, unstable weights sensitive to tiny input changes
A near-singular estimated covariance matrix, usually too few data points relative to assets (Chapter 2)

body.title: Diagnose the symptom
body.question: A quant runs the same portfolio optimization three times from three different random starting points and gets three different sets of weights, each reported as locally optimal. Which pitfall does this most likely indicate?
options: Non-convexity in the objective or constraints
A perfectly well-posed convex problem; this is normal behavior
Numerical instability from a near-singular covariance matrix
body.explanation: Chapter 2's central guarantee is that a convex problem has no local-versus-global distinction; any critical point found is the global optimum, so different starting points always converge to the same answer. Getting different locally optimal answers from different starting points is the classic signature of a non-convex problem, most likely caused by a constraint like a cardinality rule or minimum-holding threshold breaking the feasible region's convexity.

body.title: Diagnose an extreme weight problem
body.scenario: A junior analyst estimates a 60-stock covariance matrix using only 50 days of historical returns, feeds it into a minimum variance optimizer, and gets a portfolio with several weights above 300% and below -200%, funded by extreme leverage on both sides.
body.prompt: What is the most likely root cause here, using this course's terms, and what would you suggest as a fix?
body.modelAnswer: With only 50 time observations for 60 assets, the sample covariance matrix is likely close to singular, since Sigma is being estimated with fewer data points than the number of parameters it needs to pin down reliably. Chapter 2 proved genuine covariance matrices are positive semi-definite, but a matrix that is nearly singular from insufficient data behaves erratically once inverted, small estimation noise gets massively amplified into extreme, unstable weights. The standard fix is a shrinkage estimator, blending the noisy sample covariance matrix toward a simpler, more stable target, or a factor model that reduces the number of independent parameters actually being estimated from the data.

cards.definition: Different starting points converge to different, each locally optimal, answers. Traces to a cardinality, minimum-holding, or other discrete rule.
No point satisfies every constraint simultaneously; the feasible region is empty, often from contradictory rules.
An estimated covariance matrix so close to singular that small estimation noise produces extreme, unstable optimizer output, typically from too few data points relative to the number of assets.
A technique that blends a noisy sample covariance matrix toward a simpler, more stable target, reducing the extreme-weight symptom of numerical instability.

points: Non-convexity shows up as different, each locally optimal, answers from different starting points, usually from a cardinality or minimum-holding rule; the fix is reformulation or a dedicated mixed-integer solver.

Infeasibility means the feasible region is empty, often from contradictory constraints like conflicting minimum and maximum sector exposure rules; solvers report this directly, and relaxing constraints one at a time isolates the conflict.

Numerical instability from a near-singular covariance matrix shows up as extreme, unstable weights, usually from too few historical data points relative to the number of assets; shrinkage estimators and factor models are the standard fixes.

Every one of these three failure modes maps to a specific assumption from earlier in this course, convexity (Chapter 2), a non-empty feasible region (Chapter 1), or a genuinely well-behaved covariance matrix (Chapter 2), breaking down.
Diagnosing a solver failure is really just asking which of these three assumptions the current problem violates, then applying the matching fix rather than guessing.
The final lesson closes out the course with a full recap and pointers for where to go next.
